name: Bacitracin
route: Ointment applied to the skin 1-3 times a day; prescription eye ointments also exist
status: FDA-approved for topical use (OTC first-aid ointment); the injectable form was withdrawn for safety reasons in 2020-2022
mechanism: Ties up the lipid carrier bacteria use to move cell-wall building blocks, so susceptible Gram-positive bacteria cannot build their walls
uses: Preventing infection in minor cuts, scrapes and burns

article.summary: Bacitracin is a peptide antibiotic made by Bacillus bacteria, sold over the counter as a first-aid ointment for minor wounds. Its injectable form was pulled from the US market for safety.
article.takeaway: Bacitracin is one of the oldest antibiotics still on pharmacy shelves, found in plain first-aid ointment and in combination products such as Neosporin and Polysporin. It works mainly against Gram-positive skin bacteria such as staph and strep. For clean, minor wounds, a large trial found plain petroleum jelly worked about as well and caused no allergic reactions.[^1] Bacitracin is a well-known cause of **allergic contact dermatitis**, and rarely of severe allergic reactions.[^2] The injectable version was withdrawn in the US because of kidney damage and anaphylaxis risks.[^3]
glance: Approved; topical ointment sold over the counter
First aid to help prevent infection in minor cuts, scrapes and burns
Thin layer on the skin 1-3 times a day, for no more than a week without medical advice
Common contact allergen; injectable form no longer approved
[Polymyxin B](/peptides/polymyxin-b-colistin) and neomycin in combination ointments

blocks.text: Bacitracin is a mixture of ring-shaped peptides produced by certain strains of Bacillus bacteria, first described in the 1940s. To build a cell wall, a bacterium uses a fatty carrier molecule to shuttle wall components from the inside of the cell to the outside, then recycles that carrier for the next trip. Bacitracin binds the carrier at the recycling step, so the supply line stalls and the wall cannot be completed.

It is most active against Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species that commonly colonize skin. It does little against most Gram-negative bacteria, which is why it is often combined with polymyxin B, which covers that group.

items: **Over the counter:** bacitracin zinc ointment, usually 500 units per gram, for minor cuts, scrapes and burns[^4]
**Combinations:** double-antibiotic (with polymyxin B) and triple-antibiotic (adding neomycin) first-aid ointments, some with a numbing agent
**Prescription:** eye ointments, alone or combined with polymyxin B, for surface eye infections

blocks.text: Deep or puncture wounds, animal bites and serious burns need medical assessment rather than a first-aid ointment, as the product label itself states.[^4]

Bacitracin was approved long before modern trial standards, and the evidence that it improves outcomes in minor wounds is thin. In a randomized trial of 922 people treated after skin surgery, infection rates were low with both bacitracin (0.9%) and plain white petrolatum (2.0%), a difference that was not statistically significant. Four people using bacitracin developed allergic contact dermatitis and none using petrolatum did.[^1]

A broad review of topical antibiotics concluded that evidence for routine preventive use is limited, and flagged allergy to older agents such as bacitracin and growing resistance as reasons to use them selectively.[^5]

items: **Allergic contact dermatitis:** itchy redness or rash where it is applied; common enough that the American Contact Dermatitis Society named bacitracin the contact allergen of the year in 2003[^2]
**Anaphylaxis:** rare, but documented within minutes of applying the ointment to large areas of broken skin[^6]
**Neomycin combinations** add a second frequent contact allergen
**Label limits:** not for the eyes (OTC products), large areas of the body, or use beyond a week without a doctor's advice[^4]

blocks.text: Topical bacitracin remains an approved over-the-counter first-aid antibiotic. Bacitracin for injection, once used for staph pneumonia in infants, was a different story: in January 2020 the FDA asked manufacturers to withdraw it, citing kidney toxicity and anaphylaxis, and in 2022 the agency formally determined it had been withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness.[^3] Generic copies of the injection can no longer be approved.

evidence.label: Approved, but few modern trials for minor wounds
evidence.text: Bacitracin's approval rests on decades-old standards. The best randomized evidence suggests it adds little over plain petrolatum for clean surgical wounds while carrying an allergy risk,[^1] and reviews call the broader evidence base for preventive topical antibiotics limited.[^5]

faq.q: Is bacitracin better than petroleum jelly for a small cut?
faq.a: For clean, minor wounds, a large trial found infection rates were similarly low with either, and only bacitracin caused allergic reactions.[^1] Keeping the wound clean and moist matters most.

faq.q: What's the difference between bacitracin and Neosporin?
faq.a: Neosporin-type triple-antibiotic ointments contain bacitracin plus neomycin and polymyxin B. The extra ingredients widen coverage but also add another common allergen (neomycin).

faq.q: Why is my skin red and itchy where I used it?
faq.a: That can be allergic contact dermatitis, a known reaction to bacitracin.[^2] The product label advises stopping and asking a doctor if a rash develops.[^4]

faq.q: Why was injectable bacitracin taken off the market?
faq.a: The FDA concluded its risks, mainly kidney damage and severe allergic reactions, outweighed its benefits now that safer antibiotics exist.[^3] Skin ointments were not part of that action.
